tests.name: Philosophy
tests.preamble: Your philosophical worldview has been analyzed. Here is what your results say about your mindset, morals, and daily outlook:

scales.axisDesc: How you view reality and existence.

a.desc: Reality is strictly physical.
a.mindset: You trust what can be seen, measured, and proven by science. You do not get wrapped up in spiritual mysteries.
a.morals: You value concrete solutions, physical health, and comfort. To you, doing good means fixing real-world, physical problems.
a.example: If you are feeling deeply stressed, you look for logical fixes like adjusting your sleep schedule, exercising, or changing your workspace rather than looking for a spiritual reason.

b.desc: Reality goes beyond the physical world.
b.mindset: You feel deeply that there is more to life than just atoms and objects. You believe in hidden connections, energy, or a higher purpose.
b.morals: Your values are guided by a deeper inner compass or spiritual truth. You care heavily about peace of mind and the soul.
b.example: When making a major life change, you trust your intuition or look for signs in the universe, believing things happen for a reason.

scales.axisDesc: Your attitude toward society and other people.

a.desc: The individual is most important.
a.mindset: You believe that for a society to work, everyone must first take responsibility for themselves and protect their own goals.
a.morals: You think it is most honest and practical to act in self-interest. Forcing people to give up their goals for others feels wrong to you.
a.example: On an airplane, you firmly agree with putting your own oxygen mask on first before assisting anyone else. You apply this logic to wealth and happiness too.

b.desc: The community is most important.
b.mindset: You naturally view the world through a lens of shared responsibility. You think true fulfillment comes from lifting others up.
b.morals: You believe that a good life is measured by how much you help your community. Selfishness is something we must actively work to fix.
b.example: You would happily sacrifice your weekend or a portion of your income to help a friend in need or support a local neighborhood project.

scales.axisDesc: How you approach decisions and actions.

a.desc: Underlying principles are most important.
a.mindset: You believe that tracking fixed rules, honor, and pure intentions is the only correct way to live your life.
a.morals: To you, an action is either right or wrong on its own, no matter what happens in the end. Cheating or lying is always bad, even if it saves a situation.
a.example: You refuse to tell a minor lie to a client at work, even if telling that lie would save your team from a stressful corporate mistake.

b.desc: Real-world results are most important.
b.mindset: You are a problem solver who focuses on what actually works. You care about the final outcome more than rigid rules.
b.morals: You believe that if a decision leads to a good, happy, or safe result for people, then it was the right choice to make.
b.example: You happily bend a strict workplace rule if doing so allows you to fix a customer's urgent problem quickly and effectively.

scales.axisDesc: How you approach desires and personal comforts.

a.desc: Pleasure and happiness are the highest good.
a.mindset: You believe life is meant to be enjoyed. You try to maximize fun, joy, and comfort while avoiding unnecessary pain.
a.morals: You think it is completely natural and right to chase your passions, eat good food, and treat yourself often.
a.example: You regularly book spontaneous weekend trips or treat yourself to premium dinners simply because making yourself happy is your top priority.

b.desc: Self-discipline and simple living build character.
b.mindset: You find deep meaning in self-control. You think that chasing endless physical comforts distracts you from what truly matters.
b.morals: To you, true strength comes from resisting urges, living simply, and focusing on mental or spiritual growth.
b.example: You intentionally delete social media apps and opt for a minimal, low-cost lifestyle to keep your mind clear and fully focused on your long-term goals.

scales.axisDesc: Whether you believe in objective meaning.

a.desc: Meaning and morality are not built into the universe.
a.mindset: You view the universe as neutral. You do not believe that the universe has a hidden master plan or automatic rules for human behavior.
a.morals: Because there is no built-in cosmic meaning, you believe it is up to every individual to invent their own personal purpose in life.
a.example: When things go wrong, you do not waste time wondering if you are being punished by fate; you accept it as a random event and decide how to move forward yourself.

b.desc: Morality and meaning are objective truths.
b.mindset: You believe that certain actions are permanently right or wrong, and that life has a clear, real purpose we are meant to discover.
b.morals: You live by a structured standard of virtue. You feel that human beings have a duty to respect these objective moral values.
b.example: You speak up against an unfair practice at your local school board because you believe fairness is an absolute rule that must always be defended.

scales.axisDesc: What influences your life views most.

a.desc: Intellect, logic, and cold facts.
a.mindset: You process the world through careful analysis. You prefer data, clear proof, and logical reasoning over gut feelings.
a.morals: You believe decisions should be made with a cool, detached head. Letting intense emotions guide your choices leads to mistakes.
a.example: Before buying a new vehicle, you spend hours analyzing a spreadsheet comparing fuel rates, repair costs, and safety data instead of buying on style.

b.desc: Passions, gut feelings, and the heart.
b.mindset: You trust your heart. You believe that deep emotions, artistic expression, and intuition capture the true essence of life better than math.
b.morals: You believe that empathy, authentic passion, and listening to your inner emotional truth should guide your actions.
b.example: You choose a career path in the arts or a non-profit that fills you with intense inspiration, even if a corporate desk job would pay double.

scales.axisDesc: Your attitude towards knowledge and certainty.

a.desc: We should question everything and doubt claims.
a.mindset: You are naturally doubtful. You believe that human beings are easily fooled, so you rarely accept claims at face value without seeing heavy proof.
a.morals: You think it is reckless and unwise to blindly believe ideas. Keeping an open, questioning mind is a vital personal duty.
a.example: When a viral news story breaks on social media, you refuse to share it until you have personally checked multiple independent sources to verify the facts.

b.desc: Certain core truths can be known for sure.
b.mindset: You believe that solid, unshakeable facts exist in this world and that we can confidently find and rely on them.
b.morals: You value certainty, clarity, and firm foundations. Having solid beliefs gives you a stable ground to build a successful life.
b.example: You rely heavily on established laws of science or long-standing traditional wisdom to guide your daily choices without constant second-guessing.

tests.name: Economics
tests.preamble: Your economic preferences have been calculated. Here is a breakdown of your financial and structural values:

scales.axisDesc: How business and trade should be handled across borders.

a.desc: Restricted and protected trade.
a.mindset: You prefer economic safety and independence. You want to make sure your own country's workers are safe before opening borders to global competition.
a.morals: You believe a nation has a duty to protect its local factories and farms from being undercut by cheap foreign manufacturing.
a.example: You intentionally look for 'Made in my Country' tags at the store and support adding taxes to cheap imported goods.

b.desc: Unregulated global trade.
b.mindset: You view the world as a single, open marketplace. You believe free competition keeps prices low and quality high.
b.morals: To you, trade barriers slow down human progress. Buying and selling freely across countries is the fairest path to global wealth.
b.example: You love buying items smoothly from international online stores and disagree with putting extra taxes on imported goods.

scales.axisDesc: Where a country should get its vital goods.

a.desc: Global sharing and reliance.
a.mindset: You believe that countries succeed best when they specialize in what they do well and trade for everything else.
a.morals: You view global cooperation as a positive force that creates friendship, builds alliances, and stops nations from fighting.
a.example: You support importing your energy from one country and your tech components from another, believing it binds nations together safely.

b.desc: Total self-sufficiency.
b.mindset: You value security above all. You think depending on other nations for basic needs makes a country vulnerable during international crises.
b.morals: You believe a sovereign state must be able to survive completely on its own power without relying on foreign favors.
b.example: You push for massive investments in local farming and home-grown energy grids so your country never has to rely on foreign imports.

scales.axisDesc: How much power the government should have over business.

a.desc: Minimal government power over markets.
a.mindset: You believe that buyers and sellers handle markets much better than politicians. Government rules usually just complicate things.
a.morals: You value personal freedom. Forcing businesses to follow endless state rules feels like an attack on individual liberty.
a.example: You support letting private owners open businesses, hire staff, and set prices without needing to jump through complex government licensing steps.

b.desc: Strong government power over markets.
b.mindset: You believe that without a strong referee, big companies will mistreat workers, create monopolies, and cause economic crashes.
b.morals: You think the government has a clear duty to step in and manage the economy for the safety and benefit of the general public.
b.example: You firmly support strict laws that set maximum rent prices, cap energy bills, and penalize private companies that harm the public.

scales.axisDesc: How public services should be funded and set up.

a.desc: Services managed through global marketplace systems.
a.mindset: You believe that private competition on a global scale delivers the most efficient, high-tech, and modern services.
a.morals: To you, letting private companies run programs motivates them to innovate and keep quality high, which helps consumers.
a.example: You prefer a system where private global firms compete to offer the best healthcare insurance options or high-speed rail lines.

b.desc: Services owned and run by the national government.
b.mindset: You believe that essential needs like healthcare, water, and schools are rights, not products, and should never be run for corporate profit.
b.morals: You think a fair society must guarantee high-quality public systems for every single citizen, funded through general taxes.
b.example: You advocate for schools, hospitals, and railways to be owned directly by the state and kept completely free for all users.

scales.axisDesc: The primary focus of the national economy.

a.desc: Focus on finance, banking, and modern business.
a.mindset: You look toward the future. You believe that modern wealth is built through digital banking, global trade hubs, and business innovation.
a.morals: You value growth, technology, and wealth creation. A fast-moving, profitable corporate lifestyle drives human capability forward.
a.example: You support low regulations for banking startups, investment markets, and high-tech city hubs to attract worldwide wealth.

b.desc: Focus on farming, natural resources, and traditions.
b.mindset: You prefer stability and a direct connection to nature. You feel that chasing endless financial numbers creates artificial stress.
b.morals: You believe an economy should focus on real, tangible essentials like food, timber, and traditional local crafts instead of complex banking trade.
b.example: You support investing in local agriculture, small family farms, and eco-friendly industries that serve the immediate community's needs.

scales.axisDesc: How the overall market is arranged.

a.desc: An organic market that adapts naturally without set plans.
a.mindset: You believe the economy works best when it is fluid, decentralized, and allowed to change on the fly as people's habits shift.
a.morals: You think strict, top-down blueprints crush creativity. Letting groups organize themselves organically leads to genuine progress.
a.example: You support letting independent local networks, small co-ops, and freelance workers trade freely without needing official permits.

b.desc: A centralized body that carefully plans economic sectors.
b.mindset: You value order, paperwork, and clear structure. Without formal planning, resources get wasted and powerful people cheat the system.
b.morals: You believe that a highly structured administrative system ensures fairness, safety, and stable long-term results for all citizens.
b.example: You support creating an official government panel to map out the country's housing and infrastructure goals for the next five years.

scales.axisDesc: How citizens should pay taxes.

a.desc: A single tax rate for all citizens.
a.mindset: You believe true fairness means treating every individual exactly the same under the law, regardless of how much money they make.
a.morals: To you, taking a higher percentage of money from successful people acts as an unfair penalty on hard work and talent.
a.example: You support a simple system where a multi-millionaire and a retail clerk both pay exactly 10% of their annual income to the government.

b.desc: Higher tax rates for wealthy earners.
b.mindset: You believe that tax burdens should match a person's ability to pay. The wealthy can afford a higher rate without losing their basic comforts.
b.morals: You think the rich use public infrastructure more to build their wealth, so they owe a larger contribution back to support public welfare.
b.example: You support a tax bracket where top corporate executives pay a 35% tax rate, while low-wage workers pay 5% or nothing at all.

tests.name: Personality Compass
tests.preamble: Your basic behavioral traits have been mapped out. Here is what your compass location says about your daily interactions:

scales.axisDesc: How open you are to passion and how it influences you.

a.desc: Stable, grounded, and conventional.
a.mindset: You keep a cool head during daily events. You rely on standard, realistic steps to solve problems instead of getting overwhelmed by feelings.
a.views: You value emotional control and predictability. Reacting wildly to small disturbances looks childish to you.
a.example: When a household appliance breaks down, you immediately look up a repair manual online and systematically fix it without getting stressed.

b.desc: Emotional, creative, and open-hearted.
b.mindset: You experience life deeply. You are highly tuned into your own feelings and the emotional atmosphere of the rooms you walk into.
b.views: You believe that art, romance, empathy, and letting your true passions show are what make life genuinely beautiful.
b.example: You hold onto small travel tickets and handwritten notes because they connect you warmly to precious memories and the people you love.

scales.axisDesc: How competitive, diligent, and critical you are.

a.desc: Direct, organized, and focused on high standards.
a.mindset: You are goal-driven and speak your mind plainly. You have zero problem calling out errors if it means keeping work on track.
a.views: To you, honesty, hard work, and maintaining excellent results matter much more than worrying about people's brief feelings.
a.example: During a group project, you step up as leader and openly point out typos in a partner's slides to guarantee the team gets a top grade.

b.desc: Agreeable, easy-going, and cooperative.
b.mindset: You are a natural peacemaker. You prefer to blend into the group, help out quietly, and avoid unnecessary arguments.
b.views: You believe that keeping social harmony, being kind, and making everyone feel comfortable is far more important than winning every debate.
b.example: You happily let your friends pick the weekend dinner spot, even if you dislike the cuisine, just to keep the group happy and relaxed.

tests.name: Literature
tests.preamble: Your reading tastes have been cataloged. Here is an analysis of the types of worlds and narrative styles you gravitate toward:

scales.axisDesc: The level of simplicity or decorative flair in the writing.

a.desc: Subtle prose with a careful, economic use of words.
a.mindset: You love clean, direct writing. You find that brief sentences with no fancy descriptive filler hit the reader much harder.
a.views: You believe that master authors show their talent by using short, simple words that leave plenty of space for the reader's imagination.
a.example: You prefer reading short, gripping realist fiction where characters speak in brief, plain sentences rather than flowery speeches.

b.desc: Elaborate, lush, and complex sentence structures.
b.mindset: You enjoy grand, decorative language. You want to get lost in poetic, lavish descriptions that paint a beautiful picture.
b.views: To you, literature should be a decorative art form filled with rich vocabulary and deep, winding paragraphs.
b.example: You love diving into thick books filled with pages of detailed descriptions about scenery, historical rooms, and complex inner thoughts.

scales.axisDesc: The core nature of the story's setting and universe.

a.desc: Imaginary worlds built beyond physical reality.
a.mindset: You have a highly active imagination. You look for books that completely break away from our boring daily reality to build something new.
a.views: You believe that stepping into magical kingdoms or future galaxies allows us to explore human nature in an exciting way.
a.example: Your favorite books feature detailed maps of invented worlds, unique magic rules, mythical beasts, and grand heroic journeys.

b.desc: The real, authentic, and everyday world.
b.mindset: You want grounded stories. You find that looking closely at real-world events and normal human life is far more fascinating than magic tricks.
b.views: You believe that literature is at its best when it acts as an honest mirror, showing life exactly as it happens in the real world.
b.example: You actively pick up historical fiction, biographies, or realistic dramas that focus on normal families handling real-world issues.

scales.axisDesc: The underlying mood and emotional energy of the story.

a.desc: Grim, tense, and pessimistic outlooks.
a.mindset: You are drawn to serious, intense topics. You don't mind when a book explores the painful, sad, or scary sides of human life.
a.views: You believe that tragic plots or grim settings feel much more honest, deep, and artistic than forced happy endings.
a.example: You love reading dark crime thrillers, tragic histories, or stories where the characters must make difficult, heartbreaking choices.

b.desc: Triumphant, optimistic, and uplifting vibes.
b.mindset: You look for positivity. You want books that lift your mood, celebrate the beauty of life, and leave you feeling hopeful about the future.
b.views: You believe that a main goal of reading is to inspire a love for life, spread joy, and remind us that good can conquer evil.
b.example: You look for books with heartwarming family themes, inspirational journeys, and clear endings where characters find genuine happiness.

scales.axisDesc: The backdrop where the human nature is analyzed.

a.desc: Set in busy cities, factories, and modern towns.
a.mindset: You are fascinated by the fast-paced modern world. You like exploring how high-tech environments affect our minds and interactions.
a.views: You believe that crowded city blocks, modern technology, and industrial life provide the most compelling look at human behavior today.
a.example: You love mysteries set in rain-slicked city alleys, corporate towers, or sprawling modern metropolises.

b.desc: Set in country regions, small villages, and raw nature.
b.mindset: You feel a calm connection to natural settings. You prefer stories that step away from city stress to look at a simpler way of living.
b.views: You think that human nature shows its true, purest self when characters are placed close to the earth, wildlife, and small communities.
b.example: You prefer books set in quiet coastal villages, deep mountain forests, or small historic farming towns.

scales.axisDesc: The certainty of the message and moral lessons taught.

a.desc: A strong, clear message highlighting values and virtue.
a.mindset: You like clarity in your lessons. You want an author to take a firm stand on what is right and use their writing to support healthy values.
a.views: You believe that great stories should act as ethical guides, inspiring readers to be better, more honorable people.
a.example: You enjoy books where good characters are celebrated, bad characters serve as warnings, and a clear moral lesson is delivered.

b.desc: Full of irony, dark humor, and questioning rules.
b.mindset: You love witty, sharp humor. You enjoy seeing strict rules, stuffy leaders, and extreme systems get mocked by a clever writer.
b.views: To you, picking apart extreme beliefs with sarcasm and showing the absurdity of human nature is far more educational than preaching lessons.
b.example: You love reading dark comedies that poke fun at corrupt political systems, silly rules, or overly strict institutions.

scales.axisDesc: The layout structure and coherence of the story.

a.desc: Experimental, mysterious, and unusual structures.
a.mindset: You love a good mental challenge. You enjoy unusual storytelling styles that don't follow regular timelines or predictable rules.
a.views: You think that breaking standard rules of writing is highly artistic and forces the reader to think deeply and creatively.
a.example: You enjoy books that feature shifting timelines, dreamlike logic, or unique sentence layouts that challenge you to decipher the plot.

b.desc: Straightforward, orderly, and traditional styles.
b.mindset: You value clarity and order. You want a book to focus on delivering a great story directly without using annoying artistic tricks.
b.views: You believe that a story is best when it has a clear beginning, middle, and end, allowing the reader to follow along smoothly.
b.example: You prefer a classic, well-structured mystery or adventure novel where events happen in an orderly timeline with clear descriptions.

scales.axisDesc: The primary focus and purpose of the book.

a.desc: Focused on big existential questions and thinking.
a.mindset: You read to learn and ponder. You want a book to push you to examine deep truths about existence, truth, and human purpose.
a.views: To you, a book isn't worth reading unless it dives underneath the surface to tackle grand metaphysical questions.
a.example: You enjoy stories where characters spend quiet moments debating why we exist, what happens after death, or how we know what is real.

b.desc: Focused on the immediate plot and pure entertainment.
b.mindset: You read to relax and enjoy yourself. You want to get completely hooked by an exciting plot or attached to relatable characters.
b.views: You believe that the core purpose of fiction is to entertain, provide an escape, and tell an engaging, comfortable story.
b.example: You pick up a fast-paced thriller or a lighthearted small-town adventure novel simply to enjoy the ride and find out what happens next.

tests.name: Memes
tests.preamble: Your internet humor style has been calculated. Here is a description of your meme preferences:

scales.axisDesc: How comfortable you are with dark or boundary-pushing jokes.

a.desc: Shocking, boundary-pushing, and dark humor.
a.mindset: You like sharp, dark humor that tests social limits. You don't mind when jokes look at sensitive topics.
a.views: To you, nothing should be off-limits in comedy. Laughing at dark situations is a great way to handle real-life stress.
a.example: You frequently share dark, highly sarcastic comedy clips that make fun of awkward or unfortunate historical events.

b.desc: Positive, sweet, and comforting content.
b.mindset: You prefer lighthearted, positive humor. You look for content that spreads joy, kindness, and warmth across the web.
b.views: You believe that internet content should lift people up, bring comfort, and focus on sweet, safe interactions.
b.example: You regularly send cute animal pictures, uplifting text graphics, or stories of strangers doing nice deeds to your family group chats.

scales.axisDesc: The level of hidden sarcasm or directness in your humor.

a.desc: Deep layers of sarcasm and mocking trends.
a.mindset: You love multiple layers of inside jokes. You enjoy mocking typical online trends and being deeply sarcastic.
a.views: To you, direct clichés are boring. True internet comedy comes from highlighting the absurdity of web culture through bizarre parody.
a.example: You laugh at weirdly edited, nonsensical videos that mock classic, over-styled commercial ads.

b.desc: Direct, honest, and plain comedy.
b.mindset: You like straightforward jokes. You prefer content that says exactly what it means without hiding behind layers of internet sarcasm.
b.views: You think humor is best when it is clear, honest, and easily understood by anyone without needing a history of web lore.
b.example: You share a text post that describes a funny, simple situation at a local coffee shop that actually happened.

scales.axisDesc: The clarity or surreal nature of the joke format.

a.desc: Absurd, surreal, and nonsensical formatting.
a.mindset: You find completely random, weird things hilarious. You enjoy surreal imagery that breaks all standard logic rules.
a.views: You think that pure absurdity is highly creative and funny. Jokes don't need a normal setup to make you laugh.
a.example: You chuckle at a completely distorted, low-resolution image of a random kitchen object with a single out-of-context letter under it.

b.desc: Relatable and logical joke templates.
b.mindset: You want jokes to make clear sense. You like recognizable setups that follow a predictable, funny blueprint.
b.views: To you, comedy must connect directly to a recognizable reality or standard logic to be genuinely clever.
b.example: You love standard side-by-side photo formats that point out a clear 'expectation vs reality' mismatch when ordering online.

scales.axisDesc: How underground or popular your humor taste is.

a.desc: Obscure, niche, and fast-moving internet trends.
a.mindset: You are ahead of the curve online. You love underground inside jokes that only active internet users understand.
a.views: You think that once a joke format gets popular with massive public audiences, it loses its creative flavor and fun.
a.example: You use new, highly specific sticker formats on chat apps weeks before they get discovered by mainstream television programs.

b.desc: Classic, widely popular, and mainstream humor.
b.mindset: You enjoy widely understood, classic humor. You like content that has proved its value by making millions of people laugh.
b.views: To you, jokes are meant to connect people. Obscure, overly complicated rules for memes just ruin the shared fun.
b.example: You happily laugh at and share viral video clips, cute family sketches, or classic reaction images that have been famous for years.

scales.axisDesc: Whether your humor looks at society or daily personal life.

a.desc: Focused on current events, leaders, and news.
a.mindset: You view humor as a tool to examine society. You like content that highlights recent world news, laws, and public debates.
a.views: You believe mocking powerful leaders and current events is vital to keep our minds sharp and critique societal institutions.
a.example: You share a clever cartoon strip that gently mocks a recent public debate held between national politicians.

b.desc: Focused on everyday human habits and routines.
b.mindset: You look at the small details of daily life. You prefer jokes that capture the funny habits we all share at home or school.
b.views: You think the best comedy highlights our shared human flaws and daily routines, bringing people together through common habits.
b.example: You save a meme pointing out how incredibly hard it is to get out of a warm bed early on a cold winter morning.

tests.name: Political Philosophy
tests.preamble: Your foundational political philosophy has been calculated. Here is a thorough breakdown of your system preferences:

scales.axisDesc: Your overall drift towards left-wing or right-wing core views.

a.desc: A general focus on community balance and support structures.
a.mindset: You focus on fairness, group care, and fixing social biases. You want the system to help marginalized people directly.
a.views: You believe that a good society works to reduce unfair ranks and ensures that every citizen receives equal support.
a.example: You support funding local government programs that offer completely free career training to people from low-income neighborhoods.

b.desc: A general focus on individual output and tradition.
b.mindset: You focus on individual effort, personal responsibility, and protecting established local rules and institutions.
b.views: You believe that social and financial ranks naturally form when individuals use their unique skills to compete fairly.
b.example: You believe that hard work should allow you to keep what you earn, and that free choice naturally finds the most capable leaders.

scales.axisDesc: How you view the universe within your political system.

a.desc: The world is entirely physical and material.
a.mindset: You treat the world as a purely physical place governed by science. You prefer to look at real-world resources rather than spiritual ideas.
a.views: You think laws and government plans should be built entirely on hard data, logic, and proven material facts.
a.example: You want environmental or agricultural policies to be written strictly using data from scientific research teams.

b.desc: A deep spiritual or divine rule binds reality.
b.mindset: You believe that human life connects to higher spiritual values. A society lacks a solid compass if it ignores these deep truths.
b.views: You believe that a community's laws and institutions should honor spiritual wisdom or long-standing religious values.
b.example: You support keeping historic religious traditions embedded within public holidays and wanting community centers to support high spiritual virtues.

scales.axisDesc: How you view the progression of human societies over time.

a.desc: Human communities naturally march toward a better future.
a.mindset: You look forward with hope. You think that as humans gather knowledge, we naturally self-reform and fix old historical flaws.
a.views: To you, history is a positive timeline of growth. New social habits and technical tools will steadily build a near-perfect world.
a.example: You confidently believe that modern social movements will eventually eliminate deep-seated human biases and create total fairness.

b.desc: Human communities naturally decay without strict boundaries.
b.mindset: You view human history through a cautious lens. Without careful protection and discipline, societies naturally slide into bad morals and decay.
b.views: You believe that human progress is fragile. Ignoring old, proven rules causes a culture to lose its vital strength.
b.example: You worry that modern society is dropping the strict discipline and deep moral values that made past generations successful.

scales.axisDesc: How you view established social traditions and institutions.

a.desc: Old customs and institutions protect powerful ruling classes.
a.mindset: You are naturally critical of old systems. You believe that traditional laws and courts were designed to protect powerful groups while excluding others.
a.views: You believe we should look closely at and rebuild old structures to remove built-in biases against minority groups.
a.example: You support completely rewriting old institutional rules because you see them as systems of control rather than tools of true justice.

b.desc: Old customs and institutions preserve vital peace.
b.mindset: You respect ancestral wisdom. You believe that long-standing laws and cultural habits have stood the test of time for a good reason.
b.views: To you, ancestral customs are the glue that holds a community together. Throwing them away brings dangerous chaos.
b.example: You firmly oppose major, sudden changes to your country's founding constitution, believing those old guidelines preserve peace.

scales.axisDesc: How the structural setup of a community should look.

a.desc: Society should be set up as flat and equal.
a.mindset: You believe that all people are born as natural equals. Artificial rankings and power slots are broken setups that need fixing.
a.views: You want to live in a community that actively balances results so that every single person has an equal voice and fair life.
a.example: You support direct democracy networks where every community member votes on neighborhood laws instead of using a few powerful politicians.

b.desc: Society works best with orderly, clear rankings.
b.mindset: You view social layers as completely natural. Every organized group needs clear ranks, specific duties, and proven leaders to work well.
b.views: You believe that since talents differ, a natural order forms where the most capable people earn higher slots of authority.
b.example: You believe a corporate office or government department functions best when it uses a clear chain of command with experienced leaders making final choices.

scales.axisDesc: Your view on human nature and personal limits.

a.desc: Individuals should be free from community control.
a.mindset: You value total individual freedom. You think people bloom best when they can choose their own habits without community interference.
a.views: To you, arbitrary group limits based on race, gender, or strict local rules are wrong. Personal choice is the ultimate goal.
a.example: You support letting adults live whatever lifestyle or personal routine they prefer, as long as it does not physically harm anyone else.

b.desc: Society must enforce rules over individuals to survive.
b.mindset: You believe human nature can easily turn selfish or chaotic. Without collective rules, people will act on bad impulses.
b.views: You think that individual desires must sometimes be limited by a strong guide or leader to keep the entire community safe and moral.
b.example: You support strict community curfew laws or high police presence to keep local streets clean, safe, and completely orderly.

tests.name: Victimhood
tests.preamble: Your tendency for interpersonal victimhood has been evaluated. High percentage levels indicate intense tracking across these specific behavioral dynamics:

scales.name: Need for Recognition
scales.desc: A strong motivation to have your personal pain explicitly acknowledged and validated by others.
scales.mindset: You feel an intense need for confirmation when you are offended. If someone hurts your feelings, you cannot easily move past it until they look you in the eye and validate your pain.
scales.views: To you, a simple brush-off is an insult. People who hurt others have an absolute moral obligation to express deep guilt and apologize formally.
scales.example: If a coworker accidentally speaks over you in a meeting, you feel deeply upset and distracted until they send a clear follow-up text acknowledging the error.

scales.name: Moral Elitism
scales.desc: Viewing your own actions as exceptionally virtuous while viewing others as selfish or hurtful.
scales.mindset: You naturally view yourself as the exceptionally kind, giving, and long-suffering person in your relationships. You feel that you are permanently surrounded by less caring individuals.
scales.views: You believe that you contribute far more effort and honesty to others than you ever receive back, making you the constant target of people's selfishness.
scales.example: You regularly tell yourself that you are the only person who cleans up shared spaces or listens to problems, while your peers just take advantage of your gentle nature.

scales.name: Lack of Empathy
scales.desc: Focusing so heavily on your own hurt that you become oblivious to the feelings or perspective of the other side.
scales.mindset: When an argument happens, your internal focus is entirely blocked by your own distress. It becomes very difficult for you to see that the other person might also be hurting or frustrated.
scales.views: You believe that when people complain about your actions, they are just being selfish, attacking your weaknesses, or trying to manipulate the situation.
scales.example: If a close friend mentions that your recent text sounded cold, you immediately reject their view, believing they are intentionally trying to make you feel bad.

scales.name: Rumination
scales.desc: Constantly replaying past injustices and offenses in your mind instead of looking for real solutions.
scales.mindset: Your brain holds onto negative memories with a tight grip. You find yourself constantly re-living old arguments, which floods your mind with fresh, active anger over and over.
scales.views: You find it very difficult to forgive and forget. You feel that letting go of an injustice somehow excuses the bad behavior of the person who targeted you.
scales.example: You lie awake at 2:00 AM feeling intense irritation as you replay a minor, rude comment a neighbor made to you three days ago.

tests.name: Sensation Seeking
tests.preamble: Your desire for intensity and variety has been mapped. High scores highlight active tracking across these behavioral areas:

scales.name: Thrill and Adventure Seeking
scales.desc: A strong drive to participate in intense, high-stimulus physical activities and sports.
scales.mindset: You possess a high level of physical bravery. Safe, predictable routines feel boring to you, and you actively look for activities that get your adrenaline pumping fast.
scales.views: You believe that life is meant to be lived boldly. Avoiding all physical risks out of fear makes life dull and uninspiring.
scales.example: You look forward to trying extreme hobbies like skydiving, water skiing, or skiing fast down a high mountain slope.

scales.name: Experience Seeking
scales.desc: A drive to explore new mental, sensory, and cultural experiences through travel, art, and unique lifestyles.
scales.mindset: You are highly curious and open-minded. You love unpredictable lifestyles, alternative music, irregular modern art, and meeting unusual people.
scales.views: You believe that personal growth comes from exploring the unknown, trying weird foods, and stepping outside traditional comfort zones.
scales.example: You prefer going on vacation to a totally foreign city with zero pre-planned schedules or maps, completely happy to get lost and explore.

scales.name: Disinhibition
scales.desc: A tendency to look for release through wild social settings, parties, and uninhibited behaviors.
scales.mindset: You love to let loose. You feel best when you can drop all your daily social filters, act on sudden impulses, and be surrounded by wild energy.
scales.views: To you, strict social etiquette and uptight rules are boring. Heavy drinking, open discussions about sex, and wild parties are the ultimate way to have fun.
scales.example: You believe that a truly excellent party needs an abundance of alcohol flowing and crowds of uninhibited people acting free.

scales.name: Boredom Susceptibility
scales.desc: An intense dislike for repetition, predictable people, or calm domestic routines.
scales.mindset: Your mind gets restless incredibly fast. You lose patience with predictable individuals, repetitive tasks, or staying stuck at home for long periods.
scales.views: You think that being predictable is a major social flaw. People and movies should constantly offer new, shocking, or witty stimuli to be interesting.
scales.example: You absolutely refuse to rewatch a movie you have already seen once, finding the repetition completely unbearable.

tests.name: Fear
tests.preamble: Your internal anxiety triggers have been calculated. High scores show intense tracking across these specific fear sectors:

scales.name: Social anxiety
scales.desc: Anxiety triggered by public performance, evaluation, or social judgment.
scales.mindset: Your brain is highly alert to social danger. You constantly worry about making minor mistakes, looking foolish, or receiving criticism from peers.
scales.views: To you, social rejection feels like a major threat. You treat public spaces as high-pressure environments where you are constantly being watched.
scales.example: You feel an intense wave of dread and an elevated heart rate if you have to speak in public or enter a room where everyone is already seated.

scales.name: Agoraphobia
scales.desc: Anxiety triggered by environments that feel difficult to escape, like crowds or tight spaces.
scales.mindset: You feel unsafe when you lack control over your physical exit route. Large packed crowds, flights, or locked spaces make you feel highly trapped.
scales.views: You believe that safe, familiar home surroundings are the only places where you can fully relax your guard and feel secure.
scales.example: You feel a sudden wave of panic and look for the nearest exit when standing inside a packed, moving elevator or a dense concert crowd.

scales.name: Fear of bodily injury, death or illness
scales.desc: Anxiety triggered by biological threats, blood, wounds, and medical settings.
scales.mindset: You are highly sensitive to physical vulnerability and damage. Sights of injury, operations, or medical tools trigger a protective alarm in your brain.
scales.views: To you, medical environments are places of intense vulnerability, associated heavily with pain, suffering, and biological danger.
scales.example: You feel lightheaded, nauseous, or highly anxious when watching a nurse prepare a syringe for a medical injection.

scales.name: Fear of sexual/aggressive scenes
scales.desc: Anxiety triggered by raw hostility, physical fights, or explicit nudity.
scales.mindset: Your mind reacts strongly to intense conflict or raw physical exposure. Sights of bullying, dirty environments, or open nudity cause deep internal discomfort.
scales.views: You believe that public spaces and entertainment media should maintain a clean standard of taste, neatness, and peaceful behavior.
scales.example: You feel deeply uncomfortable and look away from the screen when a movie suddenly displays a raw, explicit sexual scene or a brutal street fight.

scales.name: Fear of harmless animals
scales.desc: Anxiety triggered by small crawling creatures, bugs, or reptiles.
scales.mindset: Your brain triggers an immediate, automated panic response when you see specific small creatures, even if you logically know they cannot harm you.
scales.views: You view creeping insects, mice, or snakes as deeply unpredictable, unclean, or threatening invaders of your personal space.
scales.example: You jump back, freeze, or shout for help the moment a harmless spider or crawling insect appears on your kitchen wall.

tests.name: Obsessions and Compulsions
tests.preamble: Your tendencies toward ritual behaviors and safety checks have been analyzed. High tracking indicates intense habits in these areas:

scales.name: Contamination and Washing
scales.desc: Urges to wash and clean due to intense fears of germs, dirt, and disease.
scales.mindset: You view the world as a place covered in hidden biological threats. Your mind constantly alerts you that public items are contaminated and dangerous.
scales.views: To you, absolute cleanliness is a vital shield. Allowing public dirt or animal dander to linger on your skin feels highly risky and unsafe.
scales.example: You wash your hands with hot water for several minutes immediately after handling cash or touching a public bathroom door handle.

scales.name: Dressing/Grooming
scales.desc: Urges to follow rigid, exact routines when organizing objects or handling personal care.
scales.mindset: You feel a strong mental need for perfect symmetry, order, and patterns. If a daily routine gets done out of sequence, your mind feels highly un-centered.
scales.views: You believe that maintaining strict, geometric order in your physical belongings creates safety and keeps your life running properly.
scales.example: You spend extra minutes sorting and folding your clothes in an exact, identical pattern before you allow yourself to go to sleep.

scales.name: Checking
scales.desc: Urges to recheck switches, locks, and documents due to an intense doubt of your own memory.
scales.mindset: Your brain experiences deep, chronic doubt about completed tasks. Even when you remember doing something, a voice whispers that you might have missed a detail.
scales.views: You believe that an absent-minded mistake on your part could lead to a massive, terrible disaster like a house fire or a legal error.
scales.example: You walk back into your house three separate times before work to verify that the kitchen stove dials are turned completely off.

scales.name: Thoughts of Harm
scales.desc: Worrying at length that you have caused disasters or accidentally hurt someone.
scales.mindset: You carry an overwhelming weight of personal responsibility. When you hear about local accidents or crimes, your mind invents useless worries that you are somehow to blame.
scales.views: To you, minor human errors are terrifying. You spend vast amounts of mental energy worrying that you have caused silent damage without realizing it.
scales.example: You spend hours feeling deeply anxious after reading about a local car accident, worrying that your driving somehow caused it earlier that day.

scales.name: Impulses to Harm
scales.desc: Experiencing sudden, intrusive mental urges to break things, drop items, or act wildly in public.
scales.mindset: You experience sudden flashes of scary, intrusive thoughts when placed in high-stakes environments. These thoughts shock you because they go against your real, gentle nature.
scales.views: You view these sudden flashes as frightening mental glitches that require you to hold onto your self-control with extra effort.
scales.example: You feel a sudden, weird flash of fear and a quick urge to throw your smartphone over the edge while looking down from a high bridge.
